description: Palettes derived from THE-LISTS mathematical sequences. Each palette uses a different sequence type as the source of hue spacing or hue angles.

palettes.name: Fibonacci Ratios — Indigo Base
palettes.math_notes: Fibonacci ratios converge to the golden ratio conjugate (≈0.618). Early steps give complementary (0.5=180°), triadic (0.667=240°), then progressively closer to the golden angle. The sequence discovers golden angle harmony from first principles.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Starts familiar (complementary pair), becomes stranger and more evenly spread as it converges. Interesting for time-based animations that begin with legible harmony and drift toward maximal coverage. The 8th color is nearly indistinguishable from the golden angle 8th.

palettes.name: Prime Gaps — Warm Cumulative
palettes.math_notes: Prime gaps (2,3,5,7,11,...) are differences between consecutive primes. They cluster near 2 (twin primes) and occasionally jump high (prime deserts). Gap 6 at 23→29 creates the dramatic red jump at position 8.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Warm start (golden yellow), cool middle (greens, cyans), dramatic red at the end. The twin prime pairs (gap=2) create short steps that look almost analogous; the gap=6 creates the surprise. Ideal for 8-step data visualization with narrative arc.

palettes.name: Collatz 27 — Vivid
palettes.math_notes: Collatz from 27 has one of the most dramatic trajectories: it reaches 9232 before descending. The first 10 values show the initial ascent before the peak. Each value scaled by 2.5° maps to the full hue circle.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: High-energy, chaotic-looking but deterministic. The values jump wildly between yellow-greens, blues, greens, magentas, reds. No obvious pattern — which is the point. Each color is a different 'altitude' in the Collatz ascent. Strong enough for generative art backgrounds, too chaotic for UI color coding.

palettes.name: Lucas — Twilight Spread
palettes.math_notes: Lucas sequence: L(n) = L(n-1) + L(n-2), starting 2,1. Like Fibonacci but with different initial conditions. Shares the golden ratio as its growth constant (φ ≈ 1.618). Gaps widen rapidly as the sequence grows.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Starts in the cool purple zone and sweeps through warm reds, yellows, greens, back to blues. The Lucas sequence's Fibonacci-like growth creates hue steps that accelerate — short analogous steps early, large jumps later. Twilight to daylight to dusk aesthetic.

palettes.name: Padovan — Cool Spiral
palettes.math_notes: Padovan sequence P(n) = P(n-2) + P(n-3), starting 1,1,1. Grows slower than Fibonacci (ratio converges to the plastic constant ≈1.3247 vs φ≈1.618). This slower growth means the palette takes longer to sweep the full hue circle.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Begins with three tight analogous blues-purples (Padovan starts 1,1,1 — three equal steps), then slowly accelerates. Cool start gives way to pinks, yellows, greens in a widening spiral. The 'calm then dramatic' structure is useful for tension-building in animation.

palettes.name: Tribonacci — Fast Sweep
palettes.math_notes: Tribonacci: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + T(n-3), starting 0,1,1. Growth ratio converges to the tribonacci constant ≈1.839. Faster than Fibonacci — palette sweeps more aggressively across the hue circle.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Starts in warm reds, gently moves through orange, yellow, green — then explodes across purple and cyan before looping back. The tribonacci acceleration creates a slow-then-fast sweep that feels like a thrown stone gaining momentum.

palettes.name: Perrin — Subtle Primes
palettes.math_notes: Perrin sequence P(n) = P(n-2) + P(n-3), starting 3,0,2. Mathematical curiosity: P(prime n) ≡ 0 (mod n) for all primes — this sequence knows about primes. Slower growth than Fibonacci, starts with a 0 term that creates no movement.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: The Perrin 0 term creates a color pause — the same hue appears twice. The irregular rhythm of slow steps (0,2,3,2) and then faster ones (5,5,7,10,12) creates a palette that breathes unevenly, like music with odd time signatures.

palettes.name: Prime Direct — Spectral
palettes.math_notes: Primes (2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19...) used directly as hue angles (prime × 18°). Primes have a slight bias toward certain residues mod 10 (Dirichlet's theorem) which produces subtle clustering patterns in the hue circle.
palettes.aesthetic_notes: Sweeps from orange through yellow, green, cyan, blue, violet, magenta — almost a full spectral arc in 8 steps. The gap between 7 and 11 (four prime units) creates the most visible jump, from lime green to sky blue. Surprisingly orderly for a sequence of primes.
